title: Word Order in Main Clauses
goal: Make simple Norwegian main clauses with the verb in second position, including subject-first statements, fronted phrases, yes/no questions, wh-questions, and common sentence-adverb placement.

objectives.statement: Make simple Norwegian main clauses with the verb in second position, including subject-first statements, fronted phrases, yes/no questions, wh-questions, and common sentence-adverb placement.

spans.value: Maja has arrived at a café where a Norwegian study group meets. She sees Jonas near the entrance.
Hei, Jonas. Jobber du her i dag?

blocks.translation: Hi, Jonas. Are you working here today?

spans.value: Ja, jeg jobber her hver lørdag, men i dag jobber jeg ikke lenge.

blocks.translation: Yes, I work here every Saturday, but today I’m not working for long.
Where is the study group sitting?

spans.value: De sitter vanligvis ved vinduet. Nå drikker de kaffe.

blocks.translation: They usually sit by the window. Now they’re drinking coffee.

spans.value: Nei, hun kommer ikke i dag.
Klokka ti begynner vi. Har du tid?

blocks.translation: At ten o’clock we begin. Do you have time?

spans.value: Ja, jeg har alltid tid til litt norsk på lørdager.

blocks.translation: Yes, I always have time for a little Norwegian on Saturdays.

spans.value: Maja and Jonas use several kinds of simple main clause (hovedsetning): ordinary statements, statements beginning with a time phrase, yes/no questions, and questions beginning with a question word. Their sentences look different, but the position of the present-tense verb follows a small set of dependable patterns.

sections.title: What this word order helps you do

spans.value: Norwegian word order allows you to change what comes first without losing track of the main verb. You can begin with the subject:
You can begin with another phrase, such as a time expression:
You can ask a yes/no question:
You can also begin a question with a question word:
In statements and main-clause wh-questions, Norwegian places the present-tense verb in the second
. This is commonly called the verb-second pattern. “Second” means the second sentence element, not necessarily the second individual word.
The first slot is the complete phrase i dag. Although it contains two words, it functions as one sentence element. The verb jobber occupies the second slot.

items.value: Subject-first statement: subject + verb
Fronted statement: fronted phrase + verb + subject
Yes/no question: verb + subject
Wh-question: question word or phrase + verb + subject

spans.value: Yes/no questions are the important exception to the literal idea of “verb second”: they begin with the verb.
The most straightforward Norwegian statement begins with the subject—the person or thing doing, experiencing, or being something. The present-tense verb follows immediately.

items.value: First slot: Jeg; Verb: jobber; Rest: her i dag.
First slot: Sara; Verb: kommer; Rest: klokka ti.
First slot: Studiegruppen; Verb: sitter; Rest: ved vinduet.
First slot: Vi; Verb: begynner; Rest: nå.

en.value: Sara is coming at ten o’clock.
The study group is sitting by the window.

spans.value: English sometimes uses an extra form of do or be where Norwegian uses only the present-tense verb. Do not add an extra Norwegian verb merely because the English translation contains one.
The Norwegian present tense drikker can correspond to both drink and are drinking, depending on context. The word-order pattern remains subject + verb.
Common mistake: separating the subject and verb
Avoid placing a time or place expression between the opening subject and the present-tense verb.
If the subject comes first, the verb normally comes next.

sections.title: Beginning with a time or place phrase

spans.value: Norwegian speakers often begin with information that sets the scene. In the dialogue, Jonas says:

no.value: I dag jobber jeg ikke lenge.

en.value: Today I’m not working for long.

spans.value: The first element is not the subject. It is a time phrase. The verb still takes the second slot, so the subject moves after the verb.

items.value: First slot: I dag; Verb: jobber; Subject: jeg; Rest: her.
First slot: Klokka ti; Verb: begynner; Subject: vi; Rest: .
First slot: Nå; Verb: drikker; Subject: de; Rest: kaffe.
First slot: På lørdager; Verb: møtes; Subject: gruppen; Rest: her.
First slot: Ved vinduet; Verb: sitter; Subject: studiegruppen; Rest: .

en.value: On Saturdays the group meets here.
The study group is sitting by the window.

spans.value: This movement of the subject to a position after the verb is often called
. You do not need to memorize the label to use the pattern. The practical rule is more important:

statement.value: When a simple statement begins with something other than the subject, put the present-tense verb next and then the subject.

spans.value: Compare the same message with two different openings:

en.value: The group meets here on Saturdays.
On Saturdays the group meets here.

spans.value: Both versions can describe the same event. The first element changes what the speaker presents as the starting point.
One phrase can contain several words
The verb does not have to be the second written word.

en.value: Every Saturday morning Jonas meets the study group.

spans.value: Hver lørdagsmorgen is one complete time phrase in the first slot. The verb møter follows that phrase.

no.value: På den lille kafeen møter Maja Jonas.

en.value: At the little café Maja meets Jonas.

spans.value: På den lille kafeen is one place phrase. The verb møter still occupies the second sentence slot.
Common mistake: keeping English subject–verb order after a fronted phrase
English normally allows Today I am working here. Norwegian requires the verb before the subject after the fronted time phrase.
Words such as ikke, alltid, ofte, and vanligvis are common
. They add meanings such as negation, frequency, or usual behavior.
In a simple subject-first statement, the sentence adverb normally comes after the present-tense verb.

items.value: Subject: Jeg; Verb: jobber; Sentence adverb: ikke; Rest: lenge.
Subject: Hun; Verb: kommer; Sentence adverb: ikke; Rest: i dag.
Subject: Jeg; Verb: har; Sentence adverb: alltid; Rest: tid.
Subject: De; Verb: sitter; Sentence adverb: vanligvis; Rest: ved vinduet.
Subject: Vi; Verb: møtes; Sentence adverb: ofte; Rest: på lørdager.

no.value: Jeg har alltid tid på lørdager.

en.value: I always have time on Saturdays.
They usually sit by the window.

spans.value: When another phrase comes first, the order is:

statement.value: fronted phrase + verb + subject + sentence adverb

no.value: I dag jobber jeg ikke lenge.

en.value: Today I’m not working for long.

no.value: På lørdager sitter de vanligvis ved vinduet.

en.value: On Saturdays they usually sit by the window.

no.value: På lørdager sitter de vanligvis her.

en.value: On Saturdays they usually sit here.
We often meet at the café.

no.value: Etter kurset møtes vi ofte på kafeen.

en.value: After the course we often meet at the café.

spans.value: Notice what stays stable in the fronted version: the verb comes before the subject, but the sentence adverb follows the subject.
Common mistake: putting ikke before the present-tense verb
After a fronted phrase, avoid putting ikke between the verb and subject.
The incorrect version can sound as though hun is being strongly contrasted with someone else. For the ordinary neutral meaning, use verb + subject + ikke.

sections.title: Yes/no questions begin with the verb

spans.value: Maja wants to know whether Jonas works at the café:
A yes/no question can be answered with ja or nei. In this question type, the present-tense verb comes first and the subject follows.

items.value: Verb: Jobber; Subject: du; Rest: her i dag?
Verb: Kommer; Subject: Sara; Rest: også?
Verb: Har; Subject: du; Rest: tid?
Verb: Sitter; Subject: gruppen; Rest: ved vinduet?
Verb: Begynner; Subject: dere; Rest: klokka ti?

en.value: Is the group sitting by the window?

spans.value: Norwegian does not normally add an equivalent of English do or does to make these questions. Move the Norwegian present-tense verb to the beginning.
A sentence adverb normally follows the subject in a neutral yes/no question.

en.value: Do they usually sit by the window?

spans.value: Common mistake: adding a Norwegian equivalent of do
Do not try to translate every part of Do you work here? word for word. Norwegian forms the question through word order.
The form jobber already carries the present tense. Its position tells the listener that this is a yes/no question.

sections.title: Wh-questions keep the verb in the second slot

spans.value: Some questions ask for specific information rather than a yes or no. They begin with a question word or question phrase.
Common forms in this lesson include:

en.value: Where is the study group sitting?

spans.value: The question word occupies the first slot. The present-tense verb follows, and then comes the subject.

items.value: Question element: Hvor; Verb: sitter; Subject: studiegruppen; Rest: ?
Question element: Når; Verb: begynner; Subject: dere; Rest: ?
Question element: Hvor; Verb: jobber; Subject: du; Rest: ?
Question element: Hva; Verb: drikker; Subject: de; Rest: ?
Question element: Når; Verb: kommer; Subject: Sara; Rest: ?

spans.value: A multiword question phrase still fills one first slot.

en.value: When on Saturday do you begin?

spans.value: The complete question phrase når på lørdag comes before the verb begynner.
Sentence adverbs normally follow the subject:

statement.value: question word or phrase + verb + subject + sentence adverb + rest

spans.value: The present-tense verb does not change form. Its position changes according to the clause purpose.
Common mistake: keeping statement order after a question word
The question word comes first, the verb second, and the subject follows.
Maja joins the group. A few minutes later, Sara sends Jonas a message, and Maja asks what is happening.
Nei, hun kommer ikke i dag. På søndag møter hun oss.

blocks.translation: No, she isn’t coming today. On Sunday she is meeting us.
Where are you meeting on Sunday?

spans.value: Vi møtes vanligvis her, men på søndag møtes vi på biblioteket.

blocks.translation: We usually meet here, but on Sunday we’re meeting at the library.

spans.value: The follow-up reuses the same word-order choices for a new part of the situation:

items.value: Kommer Sara senere? begins with the verb because it is a yes/no question.
Hun kommer ikke i dag has subject + verb + sentence adverb.
På søndag møter hun oss has fronted phrase + verb + subject.
Hvor møtes dere på søndag? has question word + verb + subject.
Vi møtes vanligvis her has subject + verb + sentence adverb.
På søndag møtes vi på biblioteket has fronted phrase + verb + subject.
Klokka elleve begynner vi has a multiword time phrase in the first slot, followed by the verb.

spans.value: For simple Norwegian main clauses in the present tense, choose the frame that matches your purpose:

statement.value: fronted phrase + verb + subject + sentence adverb + rest

no.value: På lørdager møtes vi ofte her.

en.value: On Saturdays we often meet here.

statement.value: question word or phrase + verb + subject + sentence adverb + rest

spans.value: Do not reduce the rule to “the verb is always the second word.” Think in sentence elements, and remember that yes/no questions begin with the verb.
Imagine that Maja is arranging a weekday meeting at the library rather than attending the Saturday café group.

options: På lørdager de sitter vanligvis ved vinduet.

På lørdager sitter de vanligvis ved vinduet.

explanation.value: Et ja/nei-spørsmål begynner med det finitte verbet. Subjektet kommer etterpå, og ikke står etter subjektet.

prompt.value: Put together the question that asks for the missing information.

explanation.value: Et spørreordsspørsmål begynner med spørreordet, fulgt av det finitte verbet og deretter subjektet.

text.value: Studiegruppen sitter et sted. Spør hvor.

prompt.value: You are writing to your classmate Maja to arrange a meeting. Wednesday at 5 p.m. at the library works for you. You cannot meet before 4:30 p.m. Ask if Maja has time and where inside the library she wants to meet. Write a message with the plan and questions.

payload.judge_prompt: Check audience-purpose, supplied-facts, and natural main-clause word order as gating criteria. Record sentence-adverb-placement-observation diagnostically. Report a verdict for every criterion id. Anchors: Must pass: «Hei Maja! På onsdag møtes vi på biblioteket klokka fem. Jeg har ikke tid før halv fem. Har du tid da? Hvor vil du møtes inne på biblioteket?» Must fail supplied-facts: «Hei Maja! Skal vi møtes på kafeen på lørdag? Jeg kan hele dagen. Skriv tilbake når du har tid.»

criteria.instruction: Writes a Norwegian message to Maja whose purpose is to arrange the meeting and obtain the missing information.
States Wednesday, 17:00, the library, and unavailability before 16:30, and asks about Maja's availability and preferred place inside.
Uses natural main-clause word order in statements, a yes/no question, and a wh-question.
Diagnostically records whether any sentence adverb is placed naturally; this criterion never controls the pass result.

prompt.value: Write four sentences: a regular statement about where you are meeting; a statement that starts with a time phrase; a yes/no question with «ofte» about whether you meet; and a question-word question with «vanligvis» about the meeting place.

payload.judge_prompt: Check four-requested-meanings, frame-specific-verb-order, required-adverb-placement. All four are gating because the task explicitly requests these meanings and demonstrations. Report a verdict for every criterion id. Accept natural Bokmål lexical and punctuation variants that preserve each requested meaning.

criteria.instruction: Includes an ordinary statement, a time-first statement, a yes/no question, and a wh-question expressing the four supplied meanings.

Places the present-tense verb after the subject in the ordinary statement, after the fronted time phrase and before the subject in the time-first statement, first in the yes/no question, and after the question word and before the subject in the wh-question.
Places ofte after the subject in the yes/no question and vanligvis after the subject in the wh-question, or uses meaning-preserving natural variants.

prompt.value: Fact: Sara arrives at ten. Write a four-word Norwegian sentence with the subject first, and use the verb «ankommer».

Uses natural yes-no question order, with the finite verb before the subject.

prompt.value: The study group is sitting somewhere in a café, but you do not know where. Ask the group a three-word question in Norwegian.

payload.judge_prompt: Check location-question and wh-question-order. Both criteria are gating because the task explicitly requests this question. Report a verdict for each criterion id. Accept any natural three-word wh-question asking where the group is, including «Hvor sitter dere?» or «Hvor er dere?», and punctuation or capitalization variants.

criteria.instruction: Asks the group in Norwegian where they are sitting.
Uses a wh-word followed by the finite verb and then the subject.
